transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-12
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Emma (Rivermark), Luis (Rivermark), Priya (Rivermark)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC sync to review latency tuning work TTFT improvements, streaming behavior, sequence length experiments, kernel choices and next steps for benchmarks and pricing. Action items assigned.

[00:00] Sofia: All right hello everyone, can you hear me?
[00:02] Emma: Yep, good morning, hearing you.
[00:04] Priya: Hi, yep hi.
[00:06] Marcus: Morning all. We'll try to keep this tight to 45.

[00:12] Sofia: Quick agenda - Marcus will go over the latest latency runs, TTFT numbers with streaming enabled, kernel/quantization matrix, then we'll review customer metrics and decide next steps. Does that look right Emma?
[00:18] Emma: That's perfect, yes. We really want to understand 95th pct and tail behavior.

[00:30] Marcus: Cool, so I pushed two new runs last night. Short summary: baseline hosted model on our default kernel with streaming off gave TTFT about 220ms median, 95th around 580ms on our 8k sequence sim. Enabling streaming dropped median to 120ms and 95th to ~320ms but increased total end-to-end time for long responses by ~6-8% because of chunking overhead.

[00:56] Luis: Wait, can you define TTFT how you measured it? Is that server-side first token or includes network?
[01:00] Marcus: Good question - this was measured server-side from request arrival to first token emitted at the runtime layer, excludes client deserialization but includes network from load balancer to runtime. So it's mostly internal, network delta minimal in our env.

[01:18] Emma: For us, the network between our app and Redwood is nontrivial, so when you share numbers please include an example with a simulated 30ms RTT.

[01:25] Marcus: Absolutely we'll add that. The other thing - we tried alternative kernels on the same GPU type; the optimized attention kernel gave lower median for long sequences but had a higher cold-start TTFT because compilation jitter and kernel load. So there's a tradeoff.

[01:45] Priya: Sorry, compilation jitter meaning JIT compile on the first run?
[01:48] Marcus: Yeah, for some kernels we see a short JIT/initialization penalty - about 80-120ms depending on model size. For production we mitigate via warm-up instances or precompile during deploy.

[02:05] Sofia: I think this is where dedicated/burst options help, because if you want guaranteed low TTFT we can keep warm instances for you and it's a pricing tradeoff.

[02:12] Priya: Right, pricing tradeoff - that matters. We'll want a clear cost delta for warm pool of say 10 GPUs vs on-demand.

[02:20] Marcus: Noted; I'll include a cost delta. Back to the runs - we also tested different sequence length trimming. For your prompt distribution (you shared avg ~750 tokens, 95th ~2400 tokens) truncating the KV cache for system prompt history reduced TTFT by about 15% for the 95th cases without hurting generation quality in our eval.

[02:46] Emma: That's promising. What about chunk-size when streaming - does smaller chunk size reduce TTFT?

[02:50] Marcus: Smaller chunks reduce time to first chunk but increase per-token overhead. In our traces a chunk size of ~64 tokens was sweetspot for your workload; going to 32 improved TTFT by 20ms but increased overall token CPU overhead ~3%.

[03:10] Luis: Is that overhead visible on GPU or CPU? We run on shared infra and worry about CPU bottlenecks.

[03:14] Marcus: Mostly CPU for serialization and scheduling, some on host memory movement. If you offload serialization steps or use binary streaming (we support a lightweight protobuf stream) you can reduce CPU overhead.

[03:30] Priya: Any regressions with hallucination or quality when you trim history?

[03:33] Marcus: We ran 200 test prompts from your eval set - slight drop in instruction-following for multi-turn context >4 turns when trimming aggressively. With TTL for prompts at 2 turns we saw negligible quality impact. We'll send the eval spreadsheet.

[03:50] Emma: Please add the exact prompt examples where quality fell off, that's critical for product.

[03:54] Marcus: Yep, we'll annotate specific prompts.

[04:00] Sofia: Quick question - you mentioned kernel choices. Which kernels did you test?

[04:03] Marcus: I tested three: default generic kernel, attention-optimized kernel (vectorized attention), and a fused-kernel path that uses lower-level CUDA kernels and better KV cache locality. The fused-kernel gave best steady-state throughput for long sequences but had worst cold TTFT unless warmed. Generic kernel is more stable for mixed sequence lengths.

[04:30] Luis: What about quantization - are you using q4/q5? Does that change TTFT?

[04:34] Marcus: We tested q4 and q5. Quantization reduces memory and can slightly improve throughput, but on some kernels it increases per-token CPU prep (dequant/depack) so TTFT is slightly higher by ~10-20ms on cold starts but similar once warmed. For your POC we recommended q5 as a balance; q4 gives cost benefits but needs extra QA for rare tokens.

[05:00] Priya: Hmm ok. Our compliance team also asked about determinism - quantization produced slightly different logits on some prompts. Is that expected?

[05:07] Marcus: Yes, small numeric differences are expected. We can run a regression suite to flag any behavior that crosses your threshold for acceptable change.

[05:18] Emma: On the streaming front - we saw you mentioned chunking increases total time for long responses. For our UX we prefer faster first token even if trailing tokens slightly slower. So we might accept the 6% tail overhead.

[05:28] Sofia: That's a good product preference to call out - we'll prioritize TTFT and streaming defaults. Marcus, can you propose default streaming chunk size and fallback?

[05:34] Marcus: Proposed defaults for Rivermark: streaming enabled, chunk size 64, KV history trimmed to last 2 user+assistant turns by default, pre-warm one instance per model variant in dedicated pool. We'll include a config guide and perf matrix.

[05:50] Luis: About pre-warm - is that something we can do inside our VPC for private deployment? We prefer private for compliance.

[05:56] Marcus: Yes, Rivermark private deployments can have warm pools; it's just a deployment config. There may be additional setup time for on-prem kernels but functionally identical.

[06:10] Priya: Any notes on autoscaling behavior with warm pools? We don't want warm pools to block scale-to-zero.

[06:15] Marcus: Our autoscaler allows reserved warm instances while allowing additional burst capacity that scales. We'll show cost model: reserved warm instances billed as dedicated, bursts billed on use.

[06:28] Emma: Can you share the raw traces you used? Timestamps, TTFT, seq lengths, kernel used per request?

[06:33] Marcus: Yes I'll push the CSV to the shared Drive. It includes per-request fields and sample prompts. Expect that by EOD.

[06:40] Sofia: Good. Any blockers from the customer side?

[06:43] Emma: We need the 95th pct prompt distribution - Marcus asked that but we'll send it. Also the compliance team wants the security doc set before we move to private.

[06:50] Sofia: I'll attach SOC2/ISO docs and an architecture note.

[06:54] Priya: One more question on kernel compatibility - if we pick fused kernel will that block fallback to a cheaper model if overloaded?

[06:59] Marcus: Not really - routing can fallback to a compatible model variant. But performance characteristics differ - we'll note expected latency deltas in the routing policy.

[07:12] Luis: About benchmarks: can we run a 24-hour soak with heap of small bursts to see tail behavior under noisy neighbor conditions?

[07:19] Marcus: Absolutely, we can schedule a soak on our staging cluster and let you observe. That would be on dedicated nodes though; for hosted we'd simulate traffic.

[07:29] Emma: Do you have a recommended config for our staging? We'll likely reuse 4 GPUs and run the mix we described.

[07:33] Marcus: I'll include a reproducible script and the perf harness.

[07:38] Sofia: Ok let's go into quick recap and next steps.

[07:42] Priya: Real quick - is Anthropic or OpenAI part of the funnel for us? We asked legal about multi-vendor.

[07:46] Sofia: They were mentioned as alternatives but not in the POC bench. We'll provide a short competitive note later.

[07:52] Marcus: Recap - I'll run kernel/quantization matrix on 8k/16k seqs, add simulated RTT, push CSV/traces, and share perf spreadsheet by 2027-10-15. I'll also include cost deltas for warm pool vs on-demand.

[08:06] Emma: We'll provide 95th pct prompt samples by 2027-10-13 and confirm whether we want private deployment test soak.

[08:14] Sofia: I'll send SOC2/ISO docs and updated pricing by 2027-10-14.

[08:20] Marcus: Any other items?

[08:22] Luis: No, we're good.

[08:24] Priya: Thanks everyone.

[08:26] Sofia: Thanks, end meeting.

Action items repeated in chat and calendar invites. Links referenced: perf spreadsheet (drive link), SOC2 pack (link), kernel tuning doc (internal link).
